bawaseer-lakshan-karan-ilaj.title: बवासीर: लक्षण, कारण और आधुनिक इलाज
bawaseer-lakshan-karan-ilaj.meta: बवासीर (Piles) के लक्षण, कारण, ग्रेड और आधुनिक बिना दर्द के इलाज — लखनऊ के UK-trained colorectal surgeon Dr. Wasif Raza से जानें। Apollo Medics, Lucknow।
bawaseer-lakshan-karan-ilaj.html:
बवासीर एक ऐसी बीमारी है जिसके बारे में लोग बात करने से कतराते हैं। लखनऊ और पूरे उत्तर प्रदेश में लगभग आधे वयस्क 50 की उम्र तक कभी न कभी इससे परेशान होते हैं — लेकिन शर्म, डर और ग़लत जानकारी की वजह से महीनों, कभी-कभी सालों तक इलाज टालता रहता है। सच यह है कि आज बवासीर का इलाज तेज़, पहले से बहुत कम दर्द वाला, और ज़्यादातर मामलों में एक दिन में हो जाने वाला है।

बवासीर क्या है?

गुदा (anus) के अंदर और बाहर ख़ून की नसें होती हैं। जब ये नसें फूल जाती हैं और परेशानी देने लगती हैं, तो उसे बवासीर या piles और haemorrhoids कहते हैं। यह दो तरह की होती है — अंदरूनी (internal), जो गुदा के अंदर होती है और आमतौर पर दर्द नहीं करती, और बाहरी (external), जो बाहर की त्वचा के नीचे होती है और सूजन या दर्द कर सकती है।

लक्षण

  • मल त्याग के समय या बाद में लाल ख़ून आना — टॉयलेट पेपर पर या बूंद-बूंद
  • गुदा के पास मस्सा या गांठ महसूस होना, जो मल त्याग के समय बाहर आए
  • खुजली, जलन या गीलापन
  • दर्द — आमतौर पर तभी जब मस्से में ख़ून जम जाए (thrombosed pile)
  • कभी-कभी कपड़ों पर mucus या हल्का दाग

कारण

  • लंबे समय तक कब्ज़ और मल त्याग में ज़ोर लगाना
  • टॉयलेट में देर तक बैठना (मोबाइल लेकर!)
  • फाइबर और पानी की कमी
  • गर्भावस्था और प्रसव
  • भारी वज़न उठाना, पुरानी खांसी
  • मोटापा और बैठे रहने वाली जीवनशैली

बवासीर के ग्रेड

ग्रेडक्या होता हैआमतौर पर इलाज
1ख़ून आता है, मस्सा बाहर नहीं आताखान-पान, दवा, banding
2मल के समय बाहर आता है, खुद अंदर चला जाता हैBanding, injection
3बाहर आता है, हाथ से अंदर करना पड़ता हैLaser, stapler, या सर्जरी
4हमेशा बाहर रहता हैHaemorrhoidectomy (सर्जरी)

आधुनिक इलाज के विकल्प

खान-पान और दवा — फाइबर (हरी सब्ज़ियां, फल, इसबगोल), 8–10 गिलास पानी, मल को नरम रखने वाली दवा, और क्रीम। ग्रेड 1 में अक्सर इतना ही काफ़ी है।

Rubber band ligation — OPD में, बिना बेहोशी के, मस्से पर एक छोटा रबर बैंड लगाया जाता है; एक हफ़्ते में मस्सा सूखकर गिर जाता है। उसी दिन काम पर जा सकते हैं।

Laser treatment — एक पतला laser fibre मस्से को अंदर से सिकोड़ देता है। कम दर्द, कोई बड़ा कट नहीं, उसी दिन घर। ग्रेड 2–3 के लिए उपयुक्त विकल्प।

Stapler surgery — एक गोल stapler मस्सों को ऊपर उठाकर जगह पर fix कर देता है। पारंपरिक सर्जरी से काफ़ी कम दर्द।

Haemorrhoidectomy — ग्रेड 4 या बहुत बड़े मस्सों के लिए सर्जरी से निकालना। सबसे पक्का इलाज, दोबारा होने की संभावना सबसे कम।

घरेलू नुस्खे और सड़क किनारे के “पक्के इलाज” से सावधान

लखनऊ में कई जगह “बिना ऑपरेशन बवासीर का पक्का इलाज” के बोर्ड दिखते हैं। इनमें अक्सर acid या अनजान दवाइयां लगाई जाती हैं, जिससे साधारण बवासीर बिगड़कर fistula या गंभीर संक्रमण बन जाती है। मैं हर महीने ऐसे मरीज़ देखता हूं। सही इलाज एक colorectal विशेषज्ञ से करवाएं।

बचाव

  • रोज़ फाइबर और भरपूर पानी
  • मल त्याग की इच्छा होने पर तुरंत जाएं, ज़ोर न लगाएं
  • टॉयलेट में 5 मिनट से ज़्यादा न बैठें
  • रोज़ 30 मिनट चलें

faqs.q: क्या बवासीर बिना ऑपरेशन ठीक हो सकती है?
faqs.a: ग्रेड 1–2 अक्सर दवा, खान-पान और banding से ठीक हो जाती है। ग्रेड 3–4 में आमतौर पर procedure की ज़रूरत होती है।

faqs.q: क्या ऑपरेशन में बहुत दर्द होता है?
faqs.a: Laser और stapler में बहुत कम। पारंपरिक सर्जरी में 7–10 दिन हल्का दर्द, जो दवा से control रहता है।

faqs.q: क्या बवासीर दोबारा हो सकती है?
faqs.a: सही इलाज और खान-पान में बदलाव के बाद बहुत कम।

faqs.q: कितने दिन में काम पर लौट सकते हैं?
faqs.a: Banding — उसी दिन। Laser — 2–3 दिन। सर्जरी — आमतौर पर 2–3 हफ़्ते।

blood-in-stool-piles-or-serious.title: Blood in Stool: When Is It Piles and When Is It Serious?
blood-in-stool-piles-or-serious.meta: Blood in stool is usually piles — but not always. Colorectal surgeon Dr. Wasif Raza explains what the colour, pattern and timing of bleeding mean, and when to see a specialist in Lucknow.
blood-in-stool-piles-or-serious.html:
Finding blood when you go to the toilet is frightening. Most people's first thought is cancer. Most people's second thought is "it's probably just piles" — and then they wait. Both reactions are understandable, and both can be wrong. As a colorectal surgeon, I see patients every week who waited months. The reassuring truth is that most rectal bleeding is caused by something minor. The important truth is that you cannot tell which kind you have by guessing.

What the blood looks like matters

Bright red blood on the toilet paper, or a few drops in the pan after passing stool. This is the classic pattern of piles (haemorrhoids) or an anal fissure. The blood is fresh because it comes from the very end of the bowel. If there is also sharp pain during stool, a fissure is likely; if there is a lump or itching, piles are more likely.

Blood mixed into the stool, or streaked through it. This suggests the bleeding is coming from higher up — the rectum or colon. Causes include polyps, inflammatory bowel disease, diverticular disease, and colorectal cancer. This pattern always needs a colonoscopy.

Dark red or maroon blood, or clots. Usually from the colon rather than the anus. Needs investigation.

Black, tarry, foul-smelling stool. This is digested blood from the stomach or small intestine — ulcers are the commonest cause. It needs an upper GI endoscopy, and if you also feel dizzy or weak, it needs emergency care today.

Symptoms that change the picture

Bleeding on its own, in a young person, with a clear cause like constipation, is usually benign. Bleeding becomes more concerning when it comes with any of the following:

  • A change in bowel habit — new diarrhoea, new constipation, or alternating — lasting more than two weeks
  • Unexplained weight loss
  • Persistent abdominal pain or bloating
  • A feeling of incomplete emptying, or needing to go urgently without passing much
  • Tiredness, breathlessness, or pale skin — signs of anaemia from slow blood loss
  • Age over 50 with new bleeding (over 45 under some guidelines)
  • A parent, sibling or child who had colorectal cancer or polyps

Any one of these alongside bleeding means you should see a colorectal specialist within a week or two — not wait to see if it settles.

Why "it's just piles" is a dangerous assumption

Piles are extremely common — up to half of adults have them by the age of 50. Colorectal cancer is also common, and rising in India, especially in people under 50. The two conditions can exist in the same person at the same time. A patient who has piles and starts bleeding naturally blames the piles. Sometimes the piles are bleeding. Sometimes a tumour a few centimetres higher is bleeding and the piles are innocent. There is no way to tell from the outside.

In the UK, where I practised for eight years, any patient aged 50 or over with unexplained rectal bleeding is referred for a specialist examination within two weeks. That rule exists because early colorectal cancer is highly curable and late colorectal cancer is not.

What happens when you see a specialist

The assessment is simpler than most people fear. I take a history and perform a gentle examination of the anus and lower rectum, which takes about a minute. In the clinic, a proctoscope — a short, narrow tube — lets me see the last few centimetres where piles and fissures live. If the bleeding pattern or your age or symptoms suggest anything higher up, I arrange a colonoscopy: a flexible camera that examines the entire colon in 20 to 30 minutes. If I find piles, they can often be treated by banding in the same session. If I find a polyp, it is usually removed on the spot.

Most patients leave with a diagnosis, a treatment, and peace of mind in a single visit.

What you can do today

  • Note the colour, amount and pattern of bleeding, and whether there is pain
  • Note any change in bowel habit or weight over the last few months
  • Increase fibre and water — this helps piles and fissures while you arrange an appointment
  • Book a specialist review — do not wait for it to "go away on its own"

faqs.q: Can stress or spicy food cause blood in stool?
faqs.a: Not directly. They can worsen piles or a fissure, which then bleed. The bleeding still needs a cause confirmed.

faqs.q: I'm 30. Can it still be cancer?
faqs.a: It is unlikely, but colorectal cancer under 50 is rising. If bleeding persists beyond two weeks or comes with other symptoms, get checked regardless of age.

faqs.q: Is colonoscopy painful?
faqs.a: No. It is usually done with light sedation and most patients describe it as far easier than they expected.

faqs.q: Can I just take piles medicine from the chemist?
faqs.a: Creams may reduce symptoms, but they do not diagnose anything. If bleeding continues after a week of simple measures, see a specialist.

colon-cancer-vs-rectal-cancer.title: Colon Cancer vs Rectal Cancer — What's the Difference?
colon-cancer-vs-rectal-cancer.meta: Colon cancer and rectal cancer are often grouped as "colorectal" — but they are treated differently. Dr. Wasif Raza, colorectal surgeon in Lucknow, explains the differences in symptoms, tests, surgery and recovery.
colon-cancer-vs-rectal-cancer.html:
Patients often arrive in my clinic having been told they have "colorectal cancer", or "bowel cancer", or "cancer of the large intestine" — and they are unsure which it actually is. The distinction matters, because although colon and rectal cancer start from the same type of cell, they sit in different places, behave differently, and are treated differently.

Where they are

The large intestine is roughly 1.5 metres long. The colon makes up most of it — running up the right side of the abdomen, across the top, and down the left. The rectum is the last 12 to 15 centimetres, sitting deep in the pelvis just above the anus. Cancer in the colon is colon cancer. Cancer in the rectum is rectal cancer. "Colorectal cancer" is simply the umbrella term.

How symptoms differ

Colon cancer, especially on the right side, often causes no bowel symptoms at all for a long time. The tumour bleeds slowly into a wide bowel, and the first sign may be tiredness and breathlessness from anaemia, or vague abdominal discomfort, or weight loss. Left- sided colon cancer more often causes a change in bowel habit, cramping, and visible blood.

Rectal cancer is closer to the exit, so it tends to announce itself earlier: bright red bleeding, a sense of needing to go urgently or repeatedly without passing much (called tenesmus), narrow or ribbon-shaped stools, and mucus. These are the symptoms most often mistaken for piles.

How the tests differ

Both are diagnosed by colonoscopy and biopsy, and both are staged with a CT scan to check for spread. The key difference is that rectal cancer needs an MRI of the pelvis. The MRI shows exactly how deep the tumour has grown, how close it is to the sphincter muscles and the surrounding tissue, and whether lymph nodes are involved. That image decides the entire treatment plan.

How treatment differs

Colon cancer is usually treated with surgery first. The affected segment of colon is removed along with its lymph nodes, and the two ends are joined. Chemotherapy may follow if the lymph nodes contain cancer. Most of this can be done laparoscopically, with a 4 to 6 day stay.

Rectal cancer is more complex because the rectum sits in a narrow, bony pelvis surrounded by nerves that control bladder and sexual function, and ends at the sphincter. For many rectal cancers, chemoradiotherapy is given first to shrink the tumour, and surgery follows 8 to 12 weeks later. The operation — total mesorectal excision, or TME — removes the rectum with its surrounding fatty envelope intact, which is what gives the best chance of cure. Laparoscopic and robotic approaches are particularly valuable here, because the camera can see into corners the human eye cannot.

For a small group of rectal cancer patients whose tumour vanishes completely after chemoradiotherapy, a "Watch and Wait" approach may avoid surgery altogether, under very close surveillance.

The question everyone asks: will I need a bag?

For colon cancer, almost never. For rectal cancer, most patients avoid a permanent stoma thanks to sphincter-preserving surgery, but some need a temporary stoma for a few months while the join heals, and a minority with very low tumours need a permanent one. This is the single most important conversation to have with your surgeon before surgery, and it is why a dedicated colorectal specialist matters.

Recovery

Colon cancer surgery: home in 4–6 days, normal activity in 3–4 weeks. Rectal cancer surgery: home in 5–7 days, normal activity in 4–6 weeks, with bowel function continuing to settle over several months.

faqs.q: Which is more serious?
faqs.a: Stage for stage, outcomes are similar. Rectal cancer surgery is technically more demanding, which is why surgeon experience matters more.

faqs.q: Can colon cancer spread to the rectum?
faqs.a: Rarely directly. Both can spread to the liver and lungs, which is why CT staging is done.

faqs.q: Do both need chemotherapy?
faqs.a: Not always. It depends on stage. Rectal cancer more often involves treatment before surgery; colon cancer more often after.

colostomy-bag-rectal-cancer.title: Will I Need a Colostomy Bag? What Rectal Cancer Patients Should Know
colostomy-bag-rectal-cancer.meta: Most rectal cancer patients do not need a permanent colostomy bag. Dr. Wasif Raza, rectal cancer surgeon in Lucknow, explains temporary vs permanent stomas, who needs one, and how sphincter-saving surgery works.
colostomy-bag-rectal-cancer.html:
Of all the questions I am asked by newly diagnosed rectal cancer patients, this is the one asked first, most anxiously, and most often. Some patients have delayed treatment because of it. So let me answer it directly: most rectal cancer patients do not end up with a permanent bag. But some do, and some need a temporary one. Here is how it works and how we decide.

What a stoma actually is

A stoma is an opening on the abdomen through which the bowel is brought to the surface, so that stool passes into a bag rather than through the anus. A colostomy uses the colon; an ileostomy uses the small intestine. Modern bags are flat, odour-proof, discreet under clothing, and changed by the patient. Hundreds of thousands of people worldwide live full, active lives with one.

Temporary stoma — the common one

When the rectum is removed and the colon is joined to the remaining rectum or anus, that join is low in the pelvis and takes time to heal. To protect it, we often create a temporary ileostomy upstream, so stool is diverted while the join heals. This is reversed in a second, smaller operation after 2 to 6 months. The patient then passes stool normally. Roughly half of patients having sphincter- saving rectal surgery will have a temporary stoma. It is a safety measure, not a failure.

Permanent stoma — when it is needed

A permanent colostomy is needed when the tumour is so low that it involves the anal sphincter muscles themselves. If the sphincter is removed, there is no way to control bowel movements, so the colon is brought out as a permanent stoma. This operation is called abdominoperineal resection, or APR. In well-selected cases it is the operation that gives the best chance of cure, and it is better to have a stoma and be cancer-free than to save the sphincter and leave cancer behind.

How we decide — the MRI

The single most important test is the MRI of the pelvis. It shows, in millimetres, how far the tumour is from the sphincter and whether the sphincter muscles are involved. A tumour 5 cm or more from the anal verge can almost always be treated with sphincter-saving surgery. Between 2 and 5 cm it depends on the MRI findings, the response to chemoradiotherapy, and the surgeon's technique. Below 2 cm, or with sphincter involvement, a permanent stoma is usually necessary.

How sphincter-saving surgery has improved

Thirty years ago, a tumour within 5 cm of the anus almost always meant a permanent bag. Three things changed that:

  • Chemoradiotherapy before surgery shrinks the tumour, often pulling it away from the sphincter
  • Total mesorectal excision (TME) allows the surgeon to dissect precisely along natural tissue planes right down to the pelvic floor
  • Laparoscopic and robotic approaches give a magnified view deep in the pelvis

Today, in specialist colorectal units, 80 to 90% of rectal cancer patients keep their sphincter.

Watch and Wait

A further option for a carefully selected minority: if the tumour disappears completely after chemoradiotherapy, surgery may be deferred under strict surveillance with regular MRI and endoscopy. If the tumour returns, surgery is done then. This avoids any stoma in patients who qualify — but it requires an experienced team and a committed patient.

Why the surgeon matters

The decision between sphincter-saving surgery and a permanent stoma depends on experience in low rectal dissection and on the MDT discussion. If you have been told a permanent bag is unavoidable, a second opinion from a colorectal specialist is reasonable to seek before surgery.

faqs.q: Can I live normally with a permanent colostomy?
faqs.a: Yes. Work, travel, exercise, swimming, and relationships are all possible. Stoma nurses provide training and support.

faqs.q: How long is a temporary stoma kept?
faqs.a: Usually 2 to 6 months, depending on healing and whether chemotherapy is given in between.

faqs.q: Will bowel function be normal after sphincter-saving surgery?
faqs.a: It improves over 6 to 12 months. Some patients have more frequent or urgent motions than before. Most adapt well.

early-signs-colorectal-cancer.title: 7 Early Signs of Colorectal Cancer You Should Never Ignore
early-signs-colorectal-cancer.meta: Colorectal cancer is highly curable when caught early. Dr. Wasif Raza, colorectal cancer surgeon in Lucknow, lists the 7 warning signs that deserve a specialist check — and who should be screened even without symptoms.
early-signs-colorectal-cancer.html:
Colorectal cancer is the third most common cancer in the world and is rising steadily in India — including, worryingly, among people in their 30s and 40s. The good news is unusually good: caught at Stage 1, more than 90% of patients are cured. Caught at Stage 4, far fewer are. The difference is almost entirely about how early it is found. These are the signs that should send you to a specialist.

1. Blood in or on the stool

The most common sign — and the most commonly dismissed as piles. Bright red blood on the paper is often piles or a fissure. Blood mixed into the stool, or dark blood, is more concerning. Any bleeding lasting more than two weeks, or any bleeding at all after 45, needs a proper look.

2. A change in bowel habit that doesn't settle

Everyone has the occasional upset stomach. What matters is a persistent change — new constipation, new diarrhoea, alternating between the two, or stools that have become noticeably narrower — lasting more than two to three weeks without an obvious cause like a change in diet or medication.

3. Feeling that the bowel never empties completely

A tumour in the rectum can create a constant sensation of needing to go, or of not having finished, even straight after passing stool. Doctors call this tenesmus. It is one of the most specific signs of rectal cancer and should never be ignored.

4. Unexplained weight loss

Losing 4–5 kg or more over a few months without trying — without dieting, without a new exercise routine — is a red flag for many cancers, including colorectal. Combined with any bowel symptom, it needs urgent investigation.

5. Persistent tiredness, breathlessness, or pale skin

A colon tumour — especially on the right side — can bleed slowly for months without any visible blood in the stool. The result is iron- deficiency anaemia. If a blood test shows low haemoglobin and low iron in a man of any age, or a woman after menopause, the colon must be examined. Anaemia is often the only sign of right-sided colon cancer.

6. Abdominal pain, cramping, or bloating that keeps coming back

Vague, recurring abdominal discomfort — particularly if it is new, if it is on one side, or if it comes with a change in bowel habit — can indicate a tumour partially blocking the bowel. Sudden severe pain with vomiting and inability to pass wind or stool may mean a complete obstruction, which is an emergency.

7. A lump in the abdomen or rectum

Less common, but a tumour can sometimes be felt — by the patient as a firm area in the abdomen, or by the doctor on rectal examination. Any new lump deserves assessment.

Who should be screened even without symptoms

Colorectal cancer develops from polyps over roughly 10 years, and polyps cause no symptoms. A screening colonoscopy finds and removes them before they turn into cancer — which is prevention, not just early detection. You should have one if:

  • You are 50 or older (45 in many international guidelines now)
  • A parent, sibling or child had colorectal cancer or polyps — start at 40, or 10 years before their age at diagnosis
  • You have ulcerative colitis or Crohn's disease for more than 8 years
  • You have a known genetic syndrome such as Lynch syndrome or FAP

What to do

If you have any of the seven signs, see a colorectal specialist rather than waiting. The assessment is quick, colonoscopy is far easier than its reputation, and the most likely outcome is reassurance. If something is found, finding it now rather than in a year is the single most important factor in your outcome.

faqs.q: Can colorectal cancer have no symptoms at all?
faqs.a: Yes — especially early, and especially on the right side of the colon. This is why screening exists.

faqs.q: Does a family history mean I will get it?
faqs.a: No, but it raises your risk, and it means screening should start earlier.

faqs.q: Is there a blood test for colorectal cancer?
faqs.a: A stool test (FIT) can detect hidden blood and is used for screening. CEA is a blood marker used to monitor known cancer, not to screen for it. Colonoscopy remains the gold standard.

gallstones-always-need-surgery.title: Gallstones — Do They Always Need Surgery?
gallstones-always-need-surgery.meta: Gallstones found on ultrasound — do you need surgery? Dr. Wasif Raza, laparoscopic surgeon in Lucknow, explains silent vs symptomatic gallstones, when to operate, why medicines don't work, and what keyhole removal involves.
gallstones-always-need-surgery.html:
Gallstones are extremely common — perhaps one adult in ten has them, and in India they are especially frequent in women and in North India. Many are discovered by accident on an ultrasound done for something else. The patient is then told "you have stones in your gallbladder" and is left wondering whether they are sitting on a time bomb. The answer depends on one thing: are the stones causing symptoms?

Silent gallstones

If gallstones have never caused pain and were found incidentally, they are called asymptomatic or "silent". The majority of silent gallstones stay silent. Studies following such patients for years show only about 1 to 2% per year go on to develop symptoms. For most people with silent stones, surgery is not necessary. We simply note them and advise you what symptoms to watch for.

There are exceptions where surgery is advised even without symptoms: very large stones (over 3 cm), a "porcelain" calcified gallbladder, and gallbladder polyps of 1 cm or more. Some patients awaiting organ transplant are also advised surgery.

Symptomatic gallstones

Once a gallstone has caused pain — even once — the situation changes. The pain is called biliary colic: a severe, steady ache in the upper right abdomen or under the breastbone, often after a fatty meal, lasting from 30 minutes to several hours, sometimes radiating to the back or right shoulder, often with nausea. After a first attack, about 70% of patients will have another within two years, and each attack carries a risk of complication:

  • Acute cholecystitis — the gallbladder becomes infected and inflamed; fever, constant pain, hospital admission
  • Bile duct stones — a stone slips into the main bile duct, causing jaundice and requiring an ERCP procedure
  • Gallstone pancreatitis — a stone blocks the pancreatic duct; a serious, sometimes life-threatening condition

For symptomatic gallstones, surgery is recommended — and sooner is better than later, because an operation on an inflamed, scarred gallbladder is more difficult than one on a quiet gallbladder.

Why not just remove the stones?

Because the gallbladder that formed them will form more. Removing the gallbladder removes the factory. You do not need a gallbladder — it only stores bile; the liver makes it, and after surgery bile simply flows straight into the intestine.

Why medicines don't work

Tablets that dissolve cholesterol stones exist, but they take 6 to 24 months, work only on small pure-cholesterol stones, and the stones return in half of patients within five years once the tablets stop. They have almost no role in modern practice. Shock-wave therapy (lithotripsy), used for kidney stones, is no longer used for gallstones because stones return.

What laparoscopic removal involves

Three or four small incisions. The gallbladder is freed and removed through one of the ports. Under general anaesthesia, 45 to 60 minutes. Most patients walk the same evening, eat the next morning, and go home within 24 hours. Light work within a week, normal activity in two. It is one of the safest and most frequently performed operations in the world.

faqs.q: Will I have to avoid oily food forever after surgery?
faqs.a: No. Most people eat normally within weeks. A few notice loose stools with very fatty food at first; this settles.

faqs.q: Can gallstones cause cancer?
faqs.a: Gallbladder cancer is rare but is associated with long-standing large stones, especially in North India. This is one reason large stones are removed even without symptoms.

faqs.q: Can I have surgery during pregnancy?
faqs.a: If necessary, yes — the second trimester is safest. Otherwise it is deferred until after delivery.

hernia-go-away-without-surgery.title: Hernia: Will It Go Away On Its Own?
hernia-go-away-without-surgery.meta: Can a hernia heal without surgery? Dr. Wasif Raza, hernia surgeon in Lucknow, explains why hernias don't go away, what happens if you wait, when watchful waiting is reasonable, and what modern keyhole repair involves.
hernia-go-away-without-surgery.html:
Many patients come to me having lived with a hernia for two, three, five years. They have tried a belt, avoided lifting, pushed the lump back in each evening. They ask the same question: can it heal by itself? The answer is no — and understanding why helps you make the right decision about when to fix it.

What a hernia is

The abdominal wall is a sheet of muscle and tough connective tissue that holds the intestines in. A hernia is a gap in that wall. Fat or a loop of bowel pushes through the gap, creating a bulge under the skin. The gap may be present from birth, or develop from years of strain, a previous surgical scar, pregnancy, obesity, chronic cough, or heavy lifting.

Why it cannot heal

Muscle and fascia do not regrow across a gap. Once the defect exists, the pressure inside the abdomen — every cough, every lift, every bowel movement — pushes against it. Over months and years the gap widens, not narrows. This is why hernias grow, and why a hernia that was "small and not bothering me" becomes large and uncomfortable.

What a belt or truss does

It holds the bulge in. It does nothing to the gap. Some people use one while waiting for surgery or if they are unfit for an operation, and that is reasonable. But it is not a treatment.

What happens if you wait

Three things, in order of likelihood:

1. It gets bigger and more uncomfortable. A larger hernia is a larger operation with a longer recovery.

2. It becomes irreducible. The contents can no longer be pushed back. This is uncomfortable and raises the next risk.

3. It strangulates. A loop of bowel gets trapped in the gap and its blood supply is cut off. Within hours the bowel begins to die. The

  • symptoms are sudden severe pain, a hard tender lump that will not go back, vomiting, and sometimes fever. This is a surgical emergency, often requiring removal of a section of bowel, and it carries a real risk to life. Femoral hernias and small-necked hernias
  • strangulate most often.

Strangulation is uncommon — published figures are under 1–3% per year for an untreated hernia — but it is the reason surgeons recommend planned repair rather than waiting for an emergency.

When watchful waiting is reasonable

If a hernia is small, causes no symptoms, and the patient is elderly or has serious heart or lung disease that makes anaesthesia risky, it is reasonable to monitor rather than operate. Many such patients never need surgery. This is a decision to make with a surgeon, not alone.

What modern repair involves

For most patients, laparoscopic (keyhole) repair: three small incisions, a mesh placed behind the muscle to reinforce the weak area, daycare or one-night stay, light work within a week, and published recurrence for inguinal hernia of around 1–4%. Incisional hernias carry a higher recurrence risk. Both sides can be repaired in one sitting if needed. Robotic repair offers additional precision for complex or recurrent hernias. Open repair remains appropriate for some very large hernias.

faqs.q: Can exercise or yoga cure a hernia?
faqs.a: No. Strengthening the surrounding muscles does not close the gap and heavy straining can make it worse.

faqs.q: Is hernia surgery urgent?
faqs.a: Planned surgery is not urgent, but earlier is simpler. Strangulation symptoms are an emergency.

faqs.q: Can a hernia come back after surgery?
faqs.a: With modern mesh repair, published recurrence for inguinal hernia is low (about 1–4%). It is higher for incisional and recurrent hernias.

is-fistula-surgery-painful.title: Is Fistula Surgery Painful? What to Expect
is-fistula-surgery-painful.meta: Worried about fistula surgery? Dr. Wasif Raza, colorectal surgeon in Lucknow, explains what happens before, during and after anal fistula surgery, how much it hurts, how long healing takes, and how to protect bowel control.
is-fistula-surgery-painful.html:
Fear of pain — and fear of losing bowel control — are the two reasons patients delay fistula surgery, sometimes for years. Both fears are reasonable, and both are mostly unfounded with modern technique. Here is an honest walk-through of what to expect.

Before surgery

At consultation I examine the fistula and note where the external opening is. For anything other than a simple low fistula, I arrange an MRI fistulogram — this shows the exact path of the tunnel, how much sphincter muscle it crosses, and whether there are hidden branches. Missing a branch is the commonest reason fistulas come back after surgery, so this step matters. You will be asked not to eat for six hours before the operation. A small enema is given on the morning of surgery.

During surgery

The operation is done under spinal or general anaesthesia — you feel nothing. It takes 30 to 60 minutes. The technique depends on the fistula:

  • Fistulotomy — for low fistulas crossing little muscle: the tunnel is laid open and left to heal from the base. Over 95% cure.
  • Seton — a soft thread is placed through the tract, allowing it to drain and the surrounding infection to settle. Often a first stage for complex fistulas.
  • LIFT — the tract is tied off and divided between the two sphincter muscles, without cutting either. My preferred approach for many
  • complex fistulas.
  • Advancement flap, VAAFT, laser (FiLaC) — sphincter-preserving options for specific situations.

How much does it hurt afterwards?

Less than most people expect. The first bowel movement after surgery is the moment patients worry about; with a stool softener it is uncomfortable rather than agonising. Pain is managed with ordinary tablets and settles substantially within 3 to 5 days. Patients who had an untreated fistula or repeated abscesses often say the post-operative discomfort is less than what they were living with.

The first two weeks

  • Home the same day or after one night
  • Warm sitz baths (sitting in warm water) two or three times a day and after each bowel movement — this is the single most useful thing you can do
  • A small dressing or pad; some discharge is normal and expected
  • Stool softeners and plenty of fibre and water
  • Desk work in 3 to 7 days; avoid heavy lifting and cycling for 2 weeks
  • A review at 2 weeks to check healing

How long until fully healed?

A fistulotomy wound heals from the inside out over 4 to 8 weeks. LIFT and flap procedures heal in a similar timeframe. A seton may stay in for several weeks or months before a second-stage procedure. You will know healing is complete when discharge stops and the skin closes.

Will I lose bowel control?

This is the risk that should guide the choice of technique. Cutting through too much sphincter muscle can cause difficulty controlling wind or loose stool. This is why a colorectal specialist maps the fistula first and chooses a sphincter-preserving technique for anything crossing significant muscle. With correct technique selection, significant incontinence is rare. Minor, temporary difficulty with wind in the first weeks is possible and usually resolves.

Will it come back?

Recurrence after fistulotomy for a simple fistula is under 5%. For complex fistulas treated with sphincter-preserving techniques it is higher — 10 to 30% depending on the method — and a second procedure may be needed. MRI mapping, correct technique, and good aftercare all reduce the risk.

faqs.q: Can I avoid surgery with antibiotics?
faqs.a: Antibiotics settle an abscess temporarily but do not close the tunnel. The fistula remains.

faqs.q: How soon can I drive?
faqs.a: When you can sit comfortably and brake sharply without pain — usually 3 to 5 days.

faqs.q: When can I resume exercise?
faqs.a: Walking immediately; gym and cycling after 2 to 3 weeks, once the wound is healing well.

laparoscopic-vs-robotic-surgery.title: Laparoscopic vs Robotic Surgery — An Honest Comparison
laparoscopic-vs-robotic-surgery.meta: Is robotic surgery better than laparoscopic? A UK-trained laparoscopic and robotic surgeon in Lucknow explains the real differences, when each is worth it, and what matters more than the technology.
laparoscopic-vs-robotic-surgery.html:
"Should I have robotic surgery?" is now one of the most common questions I am asked. The honest answer is: sometimes yes, often it makes no difference, and the surgeon matters far more than the machine. Here is what each actually involves, and how I decide.

What they have in common

Both are forms of minimally invasive surgery. Instead of one long incision, the operation is done through several small ports of 5 to 12 mm. A camera gives a magnified view inside the abdomen, and long thin instruments do the work. Compared with open surgery, both give less pain, lower infection risk, shorter hospital stays, smaller scars, and a faster return to normal life. For cancer, both give the same cure rates as open surgery — this has been proven in large international trials.

What laparoscopic surgery is

The surgeon stands at the operating table, holding the instruments directly, and watches a high-definition 2D screen. The instruments are straight and pivot at the port site. It is the workhorse of modern abdominal surgery — gallbladder, appendix, hernia, colon resection — and in experienced hands it is fast, safe, and excellent.

What robotic surgery is

The same ports and the same operation, but the instruments are held by robotic arms. The surgeon sits at a console a few feet away, looking into a 3D high-definition viewer, and controls the arms with hand and foot controls. The instruments have "wrists" that rotate 540 degrees — more than a human wrist — and the system filters out hand tremor. It is important to understand that the robot does nothing on its own. Every movement is the surgeon's.

Where robotic surgery has a real advantage

  • Deep in the pelvis — rectal cancer surgery, where the space is narrow, bony, and surrounded by nerves. The 3D view and wristed instruments make precise dissection easier.
  • Complex or recurrent hernias — where fine suturing of mesh in awkward positions is needed.
  • Obese patients — where a thick abdominal wall makes straight laparoscopic instruments harder to manoeuvre.

Where it makes little difference

Gallbladder removal, appendicectomy, straightforward inguinal hernia, and most colon resections are done superbly laparoscopically. Robotic surgery in these cases takes longer to set up and costs more without a measurable benefit to the patient.

Cost and time

Robotic surgery is more expensive — the equipment and consumables cost more. Operating time is often longer. Hospital stay and recovery are similar to laparoscopic. For an operation where the robot gives a real advantage, this is money well spent. For one where it doesn't, it isn't.

What matters more than the technology

A surgeon who does a procedure regularly, with good outcomes, using the approach they are most skilled in, will give you a better result than an unfamiliar surgeon with the newest machine. Ask your surgeon: how many of these do you do a year, which approach do you recommend for me, and why.

LaparoscopicRobotic
Incisions3–5 small ports3–5 small ports
Vision2D HD3D HD, magnified
Instrument movementStraight, pivot at portWristed, 540°
Best forMost routine abdominal surgeryDeep pelvis, complex hernia, obese patients
CostLowerHigher
Cancer outcomesEqual to openEqual to open

faqs.q: Is robotic surgery safer?
faqs.a: Not inherently. Safety depends on the surgeon and the team. Both approaches are very safe in experienced hands.

faqs.q: Does the robot operate on its own?
faqs.a: No. The surgeon controls every movement in real time.

faqs.q: Which do you recommend for me?
faqs.a: It depends on your condition, your body, and the operation. I will explain my reasoning at consultation.

piles-vs-fissure-vs-fistula.title: Piles vs Fissure vs Fistula — What's the Actual Difference?
piles-vs-fissure-vs-fistula.meta: Piles, fissure and fistula are the three most confused anal conditions. Colorectal surgeon Dr. Wasif Raza explains how to tell them apart by symptoms, what causes each, and how each is treated in Lucknow.
piles-vs-fissure-vs-fistula.html:
Patients use the word "piles" for almost any problem near the anus. In clinic, many patients who say they have piles actually have a fissure, and some have a fistula. The three conditions feel different, are caused by different things, and are treated differently — so getting the name right matters.

Piles (haemorrhoids) — the lump that bleeds

What it is: Swollen blood vessels inside or just outside the anus. Everyone has these vessels; piles are what we call them when they enlarge and cause trouble.

Key symptoms: Painless bright red bleeding on the paper or in the pan; a lump that comes out during stool and goes back on its own or with a push; itching; mucus. Pain is unusual unless a clot forms in an external pile, which causes a sudden, very tender swelling.

Cause: Straining, constipation, pregnancy, prolonged sitting on the toilet, chronic cough, heavy lifting.

Treatment: Fibre and fluids first. Banding in the clinic for Grade 1–2. Laser, stapled or surgical removal for Grade 3–4.

Anal fissure — the tear that hurts

What it is: A small split in the skin lining of the anal canal, usually at the back.

Key symptoms: Sharp, cutting pain during stool, often described as "passing glass", lasting minutes to hours afterwards; a streak of bright red blood on the paper; sometimes a small skin tag at the edge of the anus. The pain makes patients hold on, which hardens the stool and worsens the tear.

Cause: Passing a hard stool; sometimes diarrhoea; sometimes childbirth.

Treatment: Stool softeners, warm sitz baths and a prescription ointment that relaxes the anal muscle heal most acute fissures in 4–6 weeks. Chronic fissures that fail this are cured by a 10-minute day-case procedure (lateral internal sphincterotomy) with over 95% success.

Anal fistula — the tunnel that discharges

What it is: An abnormal tunnel running from inside the anal canal to an opening on the skin nearby. It almost always begins as an abscess — a painful collection of pus — which bursts or is drained, leaving a tract that never closes.

Key symptoms: Recurring boil or swelling near the anus that discharges pus or blood-stained fluid, then settles, then returns; persistent dampness or irritation; pain when sitting or during stool, particularly when the opening blocks and pus builds up. There may be a visible small hole on the skin.

Cause: Infection of a tiny gland inside the anal canal. Occasionally Crohn's disease or tuberculosis.

Treatment: Surgery is the only cure — no cream, antibiotic or home remedy closes the tunnel. The technique depends on how much sphincter muscle the tract crosses, which is why an MRI is often done first. Options range from simple laying-open (fistulotomy) to sphincter-preserving procedures like LIFT, seton, flap or laser.

Quick comparison

PilesFissureFistula
Main symptomBleeding + lumpSharp pain during stoolRecurring boil + discharge
PainUsually noneSevere, with stoolDull, worse when blocked
BleedingBright red, often dripsStreak on paperBlood-stained pus
Can heal without procedure?Grade 1–2 oftenAcute — oftenNever
Usual treatmentBanding / laser / surgeryOintment → sphincterotomySurgery

The one thing they share

All three can cause bleeding — and so can colorectal cancer. Whatever you think you have, bleeding that persists beyond two weeks needs a specialist examination to confirm the diagnosis.

faqs.q: Can I have more than one at the same time?
faqs.a: Yes. Piles and a fissure together is common.

faqs.q: Does kshar sutra cure fistula?
faqs.a: It can help some simple low fistulas but is slow and unsuitable for complex ones. Modern surgical techniques cure faster with less risk to continence.

faqs.q: Which is most urgent?
faqs.a: An abscess (the start of a fistula) with fever needs drainage within a day or two. The others can be seen at a routine appointment.

pitt-ki-pathri-ka-operation.title: पित्त की पथरी का ऑपरेशन — क्या उम्मीद करें
pitt-ki-pathri-ka-operation.meta: पित्त की पथरी (gallstones) का लैप्रोस्कोपिक ऑपरेशन कैसे होता है, कब ज़रूरी है, कितने दिन अस्पताल में रहना पड़ता है — लखनऊ के UK-trained surgeon Dr. Wasif Raza से जानें। Apollo Medics।
pitt-ki-pathri-ka-operation.html:
“डॉक्टर साहब, ultrasound में पित्त की थैली में पथरी निकली है — क्या ऑपरेशन करवाना पड़ेगा?” यह सवाल मुझसे हर हफ़्ते पूछा जाता है। पित्त की पथरी उत्तर भारत में बहुत आम है, ख़ासकर महिलाओं में। हर पथरी का ऑपरेशन ज़रूरी नहीं होता — लेकिन जब ज़रूरी हो, तो आज का लैप्रोस्कोपिक (दूरबीन) ऑपरेशन सुरक्षित, छोटा और जल्दी ठीक होने वाला है।

पित्त की थैली और पथरी क्या है?

पित्त की थैली (gallbladder) लिवर के नीचे एक छोटी थैली है जो पित्त (bile) जमा करती है — पित्त चिकनाई पचाने में मदद करता है। जब पित्त गाढ़ा होकर जम जाता है, तो उसमें पथरी बनती है। ये एक भी हो सकती है और सैकड़ों भी।

क्या हर पथरी का ऑपरेशन ज़रूरी है?

नहीं। अगर पथरी ने कभी कोई तकलीफ़ नहीं दी और किसी और जांच में संयोग से मिली है (silent stones), तो ज़्यादातर मामलों में ऑपरेशन की ज़रूरत नहीं। ऐसी पथरी में हर साल सिर्फ़ 1–2% लोगों को ही तकलीफ़ शुरू होती है।

लेकिन अगर पथरी ने एक बार भी दर्द दिया है, तो ऑपरेशन की सलाह दी जाती है — क्योंकि दोबारा दर्द होने की संभावना 70% है, और हर दौरे के साथ संक्रमण, पीलिया या pancreatitis का ख़तरा बढ़ता है।

कुछ स्थितियों में बिना लक्षण के भी ऑपरेशन की सलाह दी जाती है — 3 cm से बड़ी पथरी, थैली में 1 cm या बड़ा polyp, porcelain gallbladder।

पथरी के लक्षण

  • पेट के ऊपरी दाहिने हिस्से में या छाती के नीचे तेज़ दर्द — अक्सर तला-भुना खाने के बाद
  • दर्द का पीठ या दाहिने कंधे तक जाना
  • जी मिचलाना, उल्टी, पेट फूलना
  • ख़तरे के संकेत: बुख़ार, आंखों का पीला होना, लगातार तेज़ दर्द — तुरंत अस्पताल जाएं

सिर्फ पथरी क्यों नहीं निकालते, पूरी थैली क्यों?

जो थैली पथरी बना रही है, वह आगे भी बनाएगी। पूरी थैली निकालना ही पक्का इलाज है। थैली के बिना जीवन बिल्कुल सामान्य रहता है — पित्त लिवर से सीधे आंत में चला जाता है।

दवा से पथरी गलती है क्या?

व्यवहार में नहीं। कुछ दवाइयां छोटी cholesterol पथरी को 1–2 साल में गला सकती हैं, लेकिन दवा बंद करते ही आधे मरीज़ों में पथरी वापस आ जाती है। किडनी की पथरी तोड़ने वाली lithotripsy पित्त की पथरी में अब इस्तेमाल नहीं होती क्योंकि पथरी वापस आ जाती है।

लैप्रोस्कोपिक ऑपरेशन कैसे होता है?

  • पेट में 3–4 छोटे छेद (5–10 mm) — कोई बड़ा चीरा नहीं
  • पूरी बेहोशी (general anaesthesia) में, 45–60 मिनट
  • दूरबीन और पतले औज़ारों से थैली को अलग करके एक छेद से बाहर निकाल दिया जाता है
  • उसी शाम चलना-फिरना, अगली सुबह खाना
  • 24 घंटे में घर — कई बार उसी दिन
  • 5–7 दिन में हल्का काम, 2 हफ़्ते में सामान्य

अगर संक्रमण बहुत ज़्यादा हो, पथरी मुख्य नली (bile duct) में फंसी हो, या पहले पेट का ऑपरेशन हुआ हो, तो कभी-कभी ERCP की ज़रूरत पड़ती है या सुरक्षा के लिए खुला ऑपरेशन करना पड़ता है। ऐसा 2–5% मामलों में होता है।

ऑपरेशन के बाद खान-पान

पहले कुछ हफ़्ते हल्का, कम तेल वाला खाना। उसके बाद धीरे-धीरे सामान्य। ज़्यादातर लोग 3–4 हफ़्ते में सब कुछ खाने लगते हैं। कुछ लोगों को बहुत चिकना खाने पर शुरुआत में पतला मल हो सकता है — यह कुछ हफ़्तों में ठीक हो जाता है।

faqs.q: क्या ऑपरेशन में ख़तरा है?
faqs.a: लैप्रोस्कोपिक cholecystectomy दुनिया के सबसे सुरक्षित और सबसे ज़्यादा किए जाने वाले ऑपरेशनों में से एक है।

faqs.q: क्या गर्भावस्था में ऑपरेशन हो सकता है?
faqs.a: ज़रूरत पड़े तो हां — दूसरी तिमाही सबसे सुरक्षित है। वरना प्रसव के बाद।

faqs.q: क्या थैली के बिना चिकना खाना हमेशा बंद?
faqs.a: नहीं। कुछ हफ़्तों बाद सामान्य खाना खा सकते हैं।

faqs.q: ख़र्च कितना आता है?
faqs.a: Consultation पर आपकी स्थिति देखकर बताया जाता है। Apollo Medics में ज़्यादातर insurance और TPA स्वीकार किए जाते हैं।

what-happens-during-colonoscopy.title: Colonoscopy: What Happens, and Why It's Easier Than You Think
what-happens-during-colonoscopy.meta: Nervous about a colonoscopy? Dr. Wasif Raza, colorectal surgeon in Lucknow, walks through the preparation, the procedure, the sedation, what it feels like, and why it can prevent colorectal cancer.
what-happens-during-colonoscopy.html:
I have lost count of the number of patients who told me, afterwards, that they wished they had not spent weeks dreading it. A colonoscopy is a 20 to 30 minute procedure. The preparation the day before is the worst part. And it is the only test that can both find colorectal cancer early and prevent it by removing polyps before they turn into cancer. Here is exactly what to expect.

Why you might need one

  • Blood in the stool, or anaemia with no other explanation
  • A change in bowel habit lasting more than a few weeks
  • Screening — from age 45–50 depending on guideline, or 40 with a family history of colorectal cancer or polyps
  • Surveillance after previous polyps or cancer
  • Ulcerative colitis or Crohn's disease — to assess activity and screen for cancer
  • An abnormal stool test (FIT) or CT scan

The day before — bowel preparation

The colon must be completely clean so that I can see the lining. You will be given a laxative solution to drink in the afternoon and evening, and asked to stick to clear liquids — water, clear soup, tea without milk, apple juice — from lunchtime. The laxative works within an hour or two and you will go to the toilet many times. It is unpleasant but not painful, and it is over by bedtime. Stay near a bathroom, drink plenty of fluids, and use a barrier cream to protect the skin. Honest tip: this is the part everyone remembers, and it is genuinely the hardest part.

On the day

You arrive with an empty stomach. A nurse checks your blood pressure and places a small cannula in a vein in your hand. You change into a gown. In the endoscopy room you lie on your left side with knees drawn up. Sedation is given through the cannula — most patients are drowsy and relaxed, many doze, and most remember little or nothing of the procedure. Oxygen and monitoring are attached throughout.

The procedure itself

The colonoscope is a flexible tube about as thick as a finger, with a camera and light at the tip. It is passed gently through the anus and advanced along the whole colon — about 1.5 metres — to where it joins the small intestine. Air or carbon dioxide is used to open the bowel so the lining can be seen. You may feel some bloating or pressure, particularly at the bends; this is brief. The withdrawal, when I carefully examine every fold, takes 6 to 10 minutes.

If I find a polyp, I remove it there and then with a wire snare through the scope — not felt, because the colon lining has no pain nerves. If I see anything suspicious, I take a biopsy. If you have bleeding piles, I can band them in the same session.

Afterwards

You rest in recovery for 30 to 60 minutes while the sedation wears off. You may pass some wind — this is the air used during the procedure and is expected. You can eat normally. Because of the sedation you must not drive, operate machinery, or sign important documents for 24 hours, so bring someone to take you home. I will speak to you before you leave about what I found. Biopsy results take about a week.

Risks

Colonoscopy is very safe. Serious complications — bleeding after polyp removal, or a perforation of the bowel wall — occur in roughly 1 to 3 per 1,000 procedures and are more likely when large polyps are removed. These are treatable. The risk of not having a colonoscopy when it is indicated is far greater.

faqs.q: Will I feel pain?
faqs.a: With sedation, most patients feel nothing or mild pressure. Without sedation, some cramping at the bends. Sedation is routinely offered.

faqs.q: How often do I need a repeat?
faqs.a: If normal with no risk factors — 10 years. If polyps were removed — 3 to 7 years depending on type and number. Your report will state the interval.

faqs.q: Can I have it done if I'm diabetic or on blood thinners?
faqs.a: Yes, with adjustments to medication beforehand. Tell us at booking.
